title: Tensors: objects beyond their components
description: Distinguish a vector, covector and bilinear form through how they act and transform.
heading: When coordinates change, what makes two different arrays describe the same object?
lead: Vectors, covectors and bilinear forms transform differently because they perform different mathematical jobs; tensor notation records those jobs.
outcomes: Evaluate a covector on a vector and preserve that pairing under a basis change.
Transform vector, covector and bilinear-form components consistently.
Read a simple index contraction and distinguish a tensor from an arbitrary array.

blocks.body:
A displacement is something a particle undergoes; its coordinate column is how we describe that displacement using a chosen basis. If we make a basis vector twice as long, the same displacement needs half as much of it. The physical arrow has not shrunk. Only its numerical description has changed.

Now consider a device that takes a displacement and returns one number, perhaps the first-order change in temperature when the particle moves through a field. Such a rule is not another displacement. It acts on displacements. If a basis vector becomes twice as long, the device's reading on that basis vector doubles. Its components therefore change in the opposite way from the displacement components.

This is the distinction between a vector and a covector. A metric goes one step further: it accepts two vectors and returns a scalar such as their inner product. Once these actions are clear, their component transformation rules can be derived by insisting that the scalar answers stay the same.

The word tensor is often introduced through a formidable array of indices. We will reverse that order. First we identify what the object does, then choose a basis, and only then write indices as a compact record of the bookkeeping. This makes it possible to recognize when an array is a legitimate coordinate representation and when it is merely a table of unrelated numbers.

blocks.title: 1. A covector is a linear measuring rule
blocks.body:
Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with basis e₁,…,eₙ. A vector v has components v¹,…,vⁿ defined by $v=\sum_i v^i e_i$. A **covector** α is a linear function from V to real numbers: $\alpha(av+bw)=a\alpha(v)+b\alpha(w)$. Its value on a vector is called the pairing α(v). Covectors form the dual vector space V*.

The **dual basis** ε¹,…,εⁿ is defined by εⁱ(eⱼ)=1 when i=j and zero otherwise. Thus ε¹ extracts the first component, ε² the second, and so on. Any covector can be written $\alpha=\sum_i\alpha_i\varepsilon^i$, with αᵢ=α(eᵢ). Pairing with v gives
$$\alpha(v)=\sum_i\alpha_i v^i.$$
In matrix notation v is a column and α is a row, so the pairing is ordinary row-times-column multiplication.

For a differentiable scalar field T(x,y), the total differential at a point acts on a small displacement by $dT(\delta r)=T_x\delta x+T_y\delta y$. It is a covector because its first-order prediction is linear in the displacement. In orthonormal Cartesian coordinates the same numbers can be packaged as the gradient vector, but turning a covector into a vector uses the Euclidean inner product. In a general basis that identification needs a metric and should not be assumed from visual similarity.

As an example, let α=(2,−1) and v=(3,4). Then α(v)=2×3−4=2. The covector is the entire linear measuring rule, not just that one output. On another vector it gives another number, and on a sum it gives the sum of the readings. A vector and a covector can each be stored using n numbers, yet their definitions and their behavior under coordinate changes differ.

Upper and lower component indices will help preserve this distinction: vector components carry upper indices vⁱ, covector components lower indices αᵢ. This placement is bookkeeping for transformation behavior, not exponentiation. Until explicitly stated otherwise, sums remain written out so that no hidden convention does the conceptual work.

blocks.bridge: A covector is a linear measuring rule
blocks.meaning: A vector is an input displacement; a covector is a linear scalar-valued rule acting on such inputs.
blocks.question: What does the dual basis element ε² do to a vector?
blocks.answer: It returns the vector's second component in the corresponding original basis.

further.question: Why is a total differential a covector?
further.answer: At a fixed point it maps a displacement linearly to the first-order change in a scalar field.

further.question: Does a covector require an inner product to exist?
further.answer: No. Linear scalar-valued functions form the dual space without a metric.

further.question: Why can a gradient look identical to a differential in Cartesian coordinates?
further.answer: The Euclidean metric identifies the covector with a vector, and its identity matrix makes their component numbers match there.

blocks.title: 2. Derive the transformation rules from unchanged answers
blocks.body:
Collect basis vectors as the ordered row of objects e=(e₁,…,eₙ), so v=e v in matrix-style notation, with the second v denoting the component column. Let the new basis satisfy
$$e'=eS$$
for an invertible matrix S. Its columns give the new basis vectors in the old basis. Because the geometric vector is unchanged, ev=e′v′=eSv′. Therefore
$$v'=S^{-1}v.$$
The inverse appears because larger basis vectors require smaller components of a fixed vector.

For a covector row α, the new component α′ⱼ is its evaluation on e′ⱼ. Linearity gives
$$\alpha'=\alpha S.$$
The scalar pairing remains unchanged: α′v′=αSS⁻¹v=αv. This is a direct consistency check. Transforming both arrays with S or both with S⁻¹ would generally spoil the same physical measurement.

Take $S=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$: double e₁ and keep e₂. The vector v=(3,4) becomes v′=(1.5,4). The covector α=(2,−1) becomes α′=(4,−1). Their new pairing is 4×1.5−4=2, exactly the old value. The compensating transformations are visible without memorizing terminology.

A linear map A:V→V has a different rule. From w=Av and the vector transformation, w′=S⁻¹ASv′, so $A'=S^{-1}AS$. A bilinear form g:V×V→R is instead represented by a matrix through g(v,w)=vᵀgw. Requiring the same scalar in the new basis yields
$$g'=S^TgS.$$
These two square matrices transform differently because one outputs a vector and the other outputs a scalar after accepting two vectors.

For the ordinary Euclidean metric g=I and the same stretched basis, g′=diag(4,1). The vector v′=(1.5,4) then has length squared 4×1.5²+4²=25, matching 3²+4² in the original basis. Treating the new basis as if it were orthonormal and using I again would incorrectly give 18.25. A change in component numbers does not license a change in the measuring rule.

blocks.bridge: Derive the transformation rules from unchanged answers
blocks.meaning: Transformation laws follow from preserving the object's action, not from the shape of its array.
blocks.question: Under e′=eS, why does a vector column use S⁻¹?
blocks.answer: The equality ev=eSv′ for the same geometric vector requires v=Sv′, hence v′=S⁻¹v.

further.question: How does a covector row transform?
Why do a linear-map matrix and a metric matrix transform differently?
further.answer: A linear map has a vector output and one vector input; a metric has two vector inputs and a scalar output.

further.question: What metric describes a Cartesian basis whose first vector has been doubled?
further.answer: Starting from g=I, the new metric is diag(4,1), accounting for the squared length of the new first basis vector.

blocks.title: 3. Let indices describe multilinear structure
blocks.body:
A tensor can be understood as a multilinear object: it is linear separately in each of its relevant vector or covector inputs. A bilinear form is a covariant rank-two tensor because it accepts two vectors. Its components gᵢⱼ are its values on pairs of basis vectors. A linear map has one vector-output slot and one vector-input slot, conventionally written $A^i{}_j$. The index positions record the different transformation factors.

We now introduce the **Einstein summation convention** for this chapter and those that follow: a repeated index appearing once up and once down in a term is summed over its full range. Thus αᵢvⁱ means Σᵢαᵢvⁱ, and $w^i=A^i{}_jv^j$ means one equation for each free index i, summing over j. A free index labels the component of the result; a repeated, or dummy, index is only a summation label.

The metric pairing becomes gᵢⱼvⁱwʲ, with both i and j summed. A nondegenerate metric can turn a vector into a covector, $v_i=g_{ij}v^j$. This is called lowering an index. It is a real operation using a specified form, not a typographical adjustment. In a nonorthonormal basis the resulting component numbers generally differ. In spacetime a negative metric entry will even change a sign.

Contraction means pairing a vector-type and covector-type slot to remove them and produce an object with fewer slots. The scalar αᵢvⁱ is the simplest example. Its coordinate independence follows from the cancelling S and S⁻¹ factors we already derived. The index notation abbreviates that argument; it does not replace it.

An arbitrary table of numbers is not a tensor merely because it has two indices. For example, the rule “write the identity matrix as the metric in every basis” fails for the stretched Euclidean basis above. The array does not transform as the same bilinear form. Identity does represent the identity linear map in every basis, because S⁻¹IS=I. The same displayed array can thus be appropriate for one mathematical role and inappropriate for another.

This chapter concerns algebra at a point. Curvilinear coordinate bases can vary from point to point, creating extra issues when differentiating tensor components. We will use local metrics next, but a full theory of covariant differentiation and curvature requires more work. Keeping the present scope clear protects the basic lesson: know the object, its slots and its transformation law before manipulating its indices.

blocks.meaning: Indices encode transformation slots; contractions preserve meaning by pairing opposite types.
blocks.question: In wⁱ=Aⁱⱼvʲ, which index is summed and which labels the output?
blocks.answer: j is summed because it appears once up and once down; i is free and identifies the output component.

further.question: Is lowering an index just moving its printed position?
further.answer: No. It applies the specified metric, which can change numbers and signs.

further.question: Why is writing g=I in every basis wrong for Euclidean length?
further.answer: A general basis change need not be orthonormal, and the metric must transform as SᵀgS.

further.question: Why is writing I for the identity linear map in every basis correct?
further.answer: Its transformation is S⁻¹IS=I, reflecting its distinct vector-to-vector role.

blocks.heading: Optional: a shear is more revealing than a rescaling
blocks.body: For $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and g=I, the new basis vectors are e′₁=e₁ and e′₂=e₁+e₂. The metric becomes $g'=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Its off-diagonal terms record the nonzero inner product of the new basis vectors. A diagonal-only length formula would miss their nonorthogonality.

blocks.heading: Why a gradient and a displacement transform differently
blocks.body:
Let the old coordinate column x be related to new coordinates by $x'=Ax$, where A is invertible and constant. A displacement transforms as $\delta x'=A\delta x$. A scalar function f, however, must have the same physical change in either description:
$$df=g^T\delta x=g'^T\delta x'.$$
Substitution forces $g'=A^{-T}g$. The derivative components transform with the inverse transpose, not with A.

A one-dimensional rescaling makes this unavoidable. If $x'=2x$, the same displacement has twice the coordinate increment, while $df/dx'$ is half $df/dx$. Their product stays unchanged. The derivative is naturally a linear rule acting on displacements—a covector.

In an orthonormal Euclidean basis we often identify that rule with a gradient vector. The identification uses the metric. Outside that setting, silently treating both component lists in the same way obscures which quantity is preserved.

For a metric matrix G, the requirement $\delta x^TG\delta x=\delta x'^TG'\delta x'$ gives $G'=A^{-T}GA^{-1}$. This is a tensor transformation law derived from an invariant comparison, rather than introduced as a rule to memorise.

The shared idea is duality: one object supplies an input and another evaluates it. Tensor notation keeps these roles straight so that contractions such as df represent coordinate-independent quantities. An array becomes meaningful through those roles and transformation rules.

blocks.body: A tensor is identified by its multilinear action and consistent transformation law; components are one representation of that action.
blocks.nextConnection: Metrics will use this language to measure polar displacements and spacetime intervals without mistaking coordinate changes for changes in geometry.

data.coreIdea: A tensor is defined by how it acts and transforms, not by the rectangular array of components used in one basis. Covectors, vectors, and bilinear forms differ by what they accept and produce, while their components change in coordinated ways under a basis transformation.
data.widerConnection: This object-versus-representation discipline is necessary for metrics, spacetime, continuum fields, and coordinate-independent laws. It is the precise version of the earlier warning that a list of numbers is not itself the mathematical object.
